articles.title: Adapted families of maps
articles.statement:
Let $X$ and $T$ be topological spaces, $P$ a set,
$U = (U_\alpha)_{\alpha \in \iota}$ a family of subsets of $X$ and $k$ a natural number. A
family of maps $f : P \times X \to T$ is adapted to $U$ with bound $k$ when there is a finite
set $A$ of at most $k$ indices such that $f$ is supported on $\bigcup_{\alpha \in A} U_\alpha$.

articles.title: Morrison–Walker lemma on adapting families of maps, bi-Lipschitz case
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a
compact metric space, $T$ a metric space, $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ a convex linear polyhedron,
$(U_\alpha)_{\alpha \in \iota}$ a family of open subsets of $X$, and $\rho$ a partition of unity on
$X$ indexed by $\iota$ and subordinate to $U$. Let $f : P \times X \to T$ be continuous and suppose
that for each $p \in P$ the map $x \mapsto f(p, x)$ is a homeomorphism $h_p : X \to T$, and that for
some constant $L \ge 0$ the map $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz on $P \times X$ (for the sup metrics on
$\mathbb{R}^k$ and on $P \times X$) and every inverse $h_p^{-1}$ is $L$-Lipschitz. Then there are a
continuous map $F : [0, 1] \times P \times X \to T$, a constant $L' \ge 0$ and homeomorphisms
$H_{t,p} : X \to T$ for $(t, p) \in [0, 1] \times P$ such that: (i) $F(0, p, x) = f(p, x)$ for all
$p$ and $x$; (ii) $F(t, p, x) = H_{t,p}(x)$ for all $t$, $p$, $x$; (iii) there is a polyhedral
subdivision $K$ of $P$ such that, for every facet (maximal face) $D$ of $K$, the family
$(p, x) \mapsto F(1, p, x)$ with $p$ in the closed cell of $D$ is adapted to $U$ with bound $k$;
(iv) for every $S \subseteq X$, if $f$ is supported on $S$, then $F$, as a family with parameter
$(t, p) \in [0, 1] \times P$, is supported on $S$; (v) for every boundary subpolyhedron $Q$ of $P$
and every $S' \subseteq X$, if the restriction of $f$ to $Q \times X$ is supported on $S'$, then
the restriction of $F$ to $[0, 1] \times Q \times X$, as a family with parameter
$(t, q) \in [0, 1] \times Q$, is supported on $S'$; and (vi) every $H_{t,p}$ and every inverse
$H_{t,p}^{-1}$ is $L'$-Lipschitz.

## Sources

- S. Morrison and K. Walker, *The Blob Complex*, arXiv:1009.5025, Appendix B, Lemma B.0.1 (pp. 93–96): https://arxiv.org/pdf/1009.5025. Problem `families_of_maps_b01` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Closed cells
articles.statement:
Let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ and let $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ be a finite
set (typically the vertex set of a face of a subdivision of $P$). The closed cell of $D$ in $P$ is
the set of points of $P$ that lie in the convex hull of $D$, viewed as a subset of $P$.

articles.title: Morrison–Walker lemma on adapting families of maps to an open cover
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a compact
topological space, $T$ a topological space, $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ a convex linear polyhedron,
$(U_\alpha)_{\alpha \in \iota}$ a family of open subsets of $X$, and $\rho$ a partition of unity on
$X$ indexed by $\iota$ and subordinate to $U$ (the closed support of $\rho_\alpha$ lies in
$U_\alpha$). Then for every continuous map $f : P \times X \to T$ there is a continuous map
$F : [0, 1] \times P \times X \to T$ such that: (i) $F(0, p, x) = f(p, x)$ for all $p \in P$ and
$x \in X$; (ii) there is a polyhedral subdivision $K$ of $P$ such that, for every facet (maximal
face) $D$ of $K$, the family $(p, x) \mapsto F(1, p, x)$ with $p$ in the closed cell of $D$ is
adapted to $U$ with bound $k$; (iii) for every $S \subseteq X$, if $f$ is supported on $S$, then
$F$, as a family with parameter $(t, p) \in [0, 1] \times P$, is supported on $S$; (iv) for every
boundary subpolyhedron $Q$ of $P$ and every $S' \subseteq X$, if the restriction of $f$ to
$Q \times X$ is supported on $S'$, then the restriction of $F$ to $[0, 1] \times Q \times X$, as a
family with parameter $(t, q) \in [0, 1] \times Q$, is supported on $S'$.

## Sources

- S. Morrison and K. Walker, *The Blob Complex*, arXiv:1009.5025, Appendix B, Lemma B.0.1 (pp. 93–96): https://arxiv.org/pdf/1009.5025. Problem `families_of_maps_b01` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Boundary subpolyhedra
articles.statement:
Let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$. A subset $Q \subseteq P$ is a
boundary subpolyhedron of $P$ when $Q$ is the convex hull of a finite set of points of
$\mathbb{R}^k$, $Q$ lies in the intrinsic frontier (relative boundary) of $P$, and $Q$ is a face of
$P$: whenever a point of $Q$ lies in the open segment between two points of $P$, both of those
points lie in $Q$.

The face condition matches the paper's "convex linear subpolyhedron of $\partial P$"; without it a
single non-vertex point of the boundary of $P$ would qualify.

articles.title: Convex linear polyhedra
articles.statement:
A subset $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ is a convex linear polyhedron
when it is the convex hull of a finite set of points (equivalently, a bounded intersection of
finitely many closed half-spaces).

articles.title: Polyhedral subdivisions
articles.statement:
A polyhedral subdivision of a set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ is a
geometric simplicial complex in $\mathbb{R}^k$ with finitely many faces whose underlying space
equals $P$.

articles.title: Families of maps supported on a set
articles.statement:
Let $X$ and $T$ be topological spaces and $P$ a set. A
family of maps $f : P \times X \to T$ is supported on a set $S \subseteq X$ when it does not depend
on the parameter outside $S$: $f(p, x) = f(p', x)$ for all $p, p' \in P$ and all $x \notin S$.

articles.title: Bing's house with two rooms is contractible
articles.statement:
Bing's house with two rooms, regarded as a
subspace of $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$, is contractible.

## Sources

- Allen Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*. Problem `contractibleSpace_houseWithTwoRooms` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Bing's house with two rooms
articles.statement:
Bing's house with two rooms, in the version drawn in
Hatcher's *Algebraic Topology*, is the subset $H$ of $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \times
\mathbb{R}$ consisting of the points of $[0,4] \times [0,3] \times \{0,1,2\}$ that lie in none of
$(2,3) \times (1,2) \times \{0\}$, $(1,3) \times (1,2) \times \{1\}$ and
$(1,2) \times (1,2) \times \{2\}$ (three floors with holes), together with the inner walls
$\{1\} \times [1,2] \times [1,2]$, $\{2\} \times [1,3] \times [0,2]$,
$\{3\} \times [1,2] \times [0,1]$, $[1,2] \times \{1,2\} \times [1,2]$ and
$[2,3] \times \{1,2\} \times [0,1]$, and the outer walls $[0,4] \times \{0,3\} \times [0,2]$ and
$\{0,4\} \times [0,3] \times [0,2]$.

articles.title: Borsuk–Ulam theorem
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $S^n$ be the unit sphere in the
Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. For every continuous map $f \colon S^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ there
is a point $x \in S^n$ with $f(x) = f(-x)$.

## Sources

- K. Borsuk, Fund. Math. 20 (1933) 177–190 antipodal theorem; S. Ulam; J. Matoušek, Using the Borsuk–Ulam Theorem; Lean states `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (n+1))` to `Fin n` specialization.

articles.title: Adams' theorem on spheres that are H-spaces
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the unit sphere
$S^n$ of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ admits an H-space structure if and only if
$n = 0$, $n = 1$, $n = 3$ or $n = 7$. Here an H-space structure on $S^n$ is a continuous map
$\mu \colon S^n \times S^n \to S^n$ together with a point $e \in S^n$ such that
$\mu(e, e) = e$ and the maps $x \mapsto \mu(e, x)$ and $x \mapsto \mu(x, e)$ are both homotopic
to the identity relative to $\{e\}$.

## Sources

- J. F. Adams, 'On the non-existence of elements of Hopf invariant one', Ann. of Math. 72 (1960), 20-104; J. F. Adams and M. F. Atiyah, 'K-theory and the Hopf invariant', Quart. J. Math. Oxford 17 (1966), 31-38. See also A. Hatcher, 'Algebraic Topology', Section 4.B. Problem `hSpace_sphere_iff` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Ham sandwich theorem
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n$ be finite Borel
measures on the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$, each absolutely continuous with respect to
Lebesgue measure. Then there exist a unit vector $v \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and a real number $t$
such that for every $i$, both closed half-spaces $\{x : \langle v, x \rangle \le t\}$ and
$\{x : \langle v, x \rangle \ge t\}$ have $\mu_i$-measure equal to $\mu_i(\mathbb{R}^n)/2$.

## Sources

- A. H. Stone and J. W. Tukey, Duke Math. J. 9 (1942) 356–359 ham sandwich theorem; J. Matoušek, Using the Borsuk–Ulam Theorem; Lean states measure-theoretic Euclidean specialization with `μ i ≪ volume` making the bisecting hyperplane null.

articles.title: The fundamental group of the circle is infinite cyclic
articles.statement:
The fundamental group of the unit
circle in $\mathbb{C}$ based at $1$ is isomorphic, as a group, to the additive group $\mathbb{Z}$.

## Sources

- Classical theorem in algebraic topology. Problem `pi1_circle_mulEquiv_int` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: The sixth homotopy group of the 3-sphere
articles.statement:
Let $S^3$ be the unit sphere in Euclidean space
$\mathbb{R}^4$. For every point $x \in S^3$, the homotopy group $\pi_6(S^3, x)$ is isomorphic as a
group to the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/12$.

## Sources

- H. Toda, 'Composition Methods in Homotopy Groups of Spheres', Annals of Mathematics Studies 49, Princeton University Press, 1962. The value pi_6(S^3) = Z/12 also appears in the tables of A. Hatcher, 'Algebraic Topology', Section 4.1. Problem `pi6_sphere_three_mulEquiv_zmod_twelve` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: First homology is the abelianized fundamental group
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a path-connected
topological space and let $x \in X$. Then the abelianization of the fundamental group
$\pi_1(X, x)$ is isomorphic, as a group, to the first integral singular homology group
$H_1(X; \mathbb{Z})$ of $X$.

## Sources

- W. Hurewicz (1935); see Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*, Theorem 2A.1. Knill, *Some fundamental theorems in mathematics*, §153. Problem `hurewicz_h1_abelianization` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Integral singular homology
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and a topological space $X$,
$H_n(X; \mathbb{Z})$ denotes the $n$-th singular homology group of $X$ with coefficients in
$\mathbb{Z}$, regarded as an abelian group.

articles.title: The category of spaces admitting a CW structure
articles.statement:
The full subcategory of the category of
topological spaces whose objects are the spaces $X$ admitting a classical CW complex structure
with underlying set all of $X$; its morphisms are all continuous maps between such spaces.

articles.title: Comparison map for the derived inclusion
articles.statement:
Let $\iota$ be the inclusion of light solid
abelian groups into light condensed abelian groups, $D(\iota)$ the induced derived inclusion, and
$Q$ the localization functors from cochain complexes to derived categories. The comparison map is
the natural transformation from $K \mapsto Q(\iota K)$ to $K \mapsto D(\iota)(Q K)$, for cochain
complexes $K$ of light solid abelian groups, where $\iota K$ is $K$ with $\iota$ applied
degreewise; it is the inverse of the natural isomorphism $D(\iota)(Q K) \cong Q(\iota K)$.

With this comparison map, $D(\iota)$ is a right derived functor of the degreewise inclusion with
respect to quasi-isomorphisms.

articles.title: The derived inclusion is computed degreewise
articles.statement:
Let $\iota$ be the inclusion of light solid
abelian groups into light condensed abelian groups, $D(\iota)$ the induced derived inclusion, and
$Q$ the localization functors from cochain complexes to derived categories. This is the natural
isomorphism $D(\iota)(Q K) \cong Q(\iota K)$ for cochain complexes $K$ of light solid abelian
groups, where $\iota K$ is $K$ with $\iota$ applied degreewise.

articles.title: Derived inclusion of solid abelian groups
articles.statement:
The inclusion $\iota$ of light solid abelian
groups into light condensed abelian groups is exact, so it induces a functor $D(\iota)$ from the
derived category of light solid abelian groups to the derived category of light condensed abelian
groups.

articles.title: Derived solidification is left adjoint to the derived inclusion
articles.statement:
An adjunction in which
derived solidification, from the derived category of light condensed abelian groups to the derived
category of light solid abelian groups, is left adjoint to the derived inclusion $D(\iota)$ induced
by the inclusion $\iota$ of light solid abelian groups into light condensed abelian groups.

## Sources

- https://github.com/dagurtomas/LeanCondensed; D. Clausen and P. Scholze, lectures on analytic stacks and light condensed mathematics.; P. Scholze, Lectures on Condensed Mathematics, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.03658. Problem `derived_solidification_free_CW_homology` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Comparison map from derived to degreewise solidification
articles.statement:
Let $Q$ denote the localization
functors from cochain complexes to derived categories. This is a natural transformation from the
functor sending a cochain complex $K$ of light condensed abelian groups to the derived
solidification of $Q(K)$ to the functor sending $K$ to $Q(\mathrm{Sol}(K))$, where
$\mathrm{Sol}(K)$ is the complex of light solid abelian groups obtained by applying solidification
to $K$ degreewise.

## Sources

- https://github.com/dagurtomas/LeanCondensed; D. Clausen and P. Scholze, lectures on analytic stacks and light condensed mathematics.; P. Scholze, Lectures on Condensed Mathematics, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.03658. Problem `derived_solidification_free_CW_homology` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: The pointwise derived comparison is the component of the natural one
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a
topological space with a CW complex structure on all of $X$, regarded as an object of the category
of spaces admitting a CW structure, and let $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be the free light condensed abelian
group on $X$. Let $F$ be the derived solidification functor on spaces admitting a CW structure,
let $\sigma$ be the natural isomorphism from $F$ to the functor sending $X$ to the derived
inclusion of the derived solidification of $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ placed in degree $0$, and let $\nu$ be
the natural isomorphism from $F$ to the integral singular chain complex functor with values in the
derived category of light condensed abelian groups. Then the pointwise isomorphism $\phi_X$ from
the derived inclusion of the derived solidification of $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ (placed in degree $0$) to
the singular chain complex of $X$ equals $\nu_X \circ \sigma_X^{-1}$.

articles.title: Pointwise derived comparison for CW complexes
articles.statement:
For a topological space $X$ with a CW
complex structure on all of $X$, an isomorphism in the derived category of light condensed abelian
groups from the derived inclusion of the derived solidification of the free light condensed
abelian group $\mathbb{Z}[X]$, placed in degree $0$, to the integral singular chain complex of $X$,
viewed as a complex of discrete light condensed abelian groups with chains of degree $n$ placed in
cohomological degree $-n$.

articles.title: Derived solidification of free CW complexes computes singular chains
articles.statement:
A natural
isomorphism of functors from the category of spaces admitting a CW structure to the derived
category of light condensed abelian groups, from the derived solidification functor $F$ to the
integral singular chain complex functor. Here $F(X)$ is the derived inclusion of the derived
solidification of the free light condensed abelian group $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ placed in degree $0$ (up
to a specified natural isomorphism), and the singular chain complex of $X$ is viewed as a complex
of discrete light condensed abelian groups with chains of degree $n$ in cohomological degree $-n$.

## Sources

- https://github.com/dagurtomas/LeanCondensed; D. Clausen and P. Scholze, lectures on analytic stacks and light condensed mathematics.; P. Scholze, Lectures on Condensed Mathematics, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.03658. Problem `derived_solidification_free_CW_homology` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Homology of the derived solidification of a free CW complex
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a topological space
with a CW complex structure on all of $X$, let $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be the free light condensed abelian
group on $X$, and let $n$ be a natural number. Then the cohomology in degree $-n$ of the derived
solidification of $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ placed in degree $0$, a light solid abelian group regarded as a
light condensed abelian group, is isomorphic to the integral singular homology group
$H_n(X; \mathbb{Z})$ viewed as a discrete light condensed abelian group.

## Sources

- https://github.com/dagurtomas/LeanCondensed; D. Clausen and P. Scholze, lectures on analytic stacks and light condensed mathematics.; P. Scholze, Lectures on Condensed Mathematics, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.03658. Problem `derived_solidification_free_CW_homology` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Derived solidification computes singular homology
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a topological space
equipped with a CW complex structure, let $n$ be a natural number, and let $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be the
free light condensed abelian group on $X$, viewed as a complex concentrated in degree $0$ in the
derived category of light condensed abelian groups. Apply derived solidification to
$\mathbb{Z}[X]$, take the homology in cohomological degree $-n$, which is a light solid abelian
group, and regard it as a light condensed abelian group. This is an isomorphism between the
resulting light condensed abelian group and the $n$-th singular homology group $H_n(X; \mathbb{Z})$
of $X$ with integer coefficients, regarded as a discrete light condensed abelian group.

The derived category is cohomologically indexed, so the $n$-th homology group sits in degree $-n$.

## Sources

- https://github.com/dagurtomas/LeanCondensed; D. Clausen and P. Scholze, lectures on analytic stacks and light condensed mathematics.; P. Scholze, Lectures on Condensed Mathematics, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.03658. Problem `derived_solidification_free_CW_homology` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Natural isomorphism specifying derived solidification on CW complexes
articles.statement:
A natural
isomorphism between the derived solidification functor on CW complexes and the composite functor
that sends a topological space $X$ admitting a CW complex structure to the free light condensed
abelian group $\mathbb{Z}[X]$, views it as a complex concentrated in degree $0$ in the derived
category of light condensed abelian groups, applies derived solidification, and then applies the
derived inclusion of light solid abelian groups into light condensed abelian groups. Both are
functors from the category of topological spaces admitting a CW complex structure, with all
continuous maps as morphisms, to the derived category of light condensed abelian groups.

## Sources

- https://github.com/dagurtomas/LeanCondensed; D. Clausen and P. Scholze, lectures on analytic stacks and light condensed mathematics.; P. Scholze, Lectures on Condensed Mathematics, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.03658. Problem `derived_solidification_free_CW_homology` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Derived solidification on CW complexes
articles.statement:
A functor from the category of topological spaces
admitting a CW complex structure, with all continuous maps as morphisms, to the derived category
of light condensed abelian groups.

A separate specification identifies it, up to natural isomorphism, with the functor sending $X$
to the derived inclusion of the derived solidification of the free light condensed abelian group
$\mathbb{Z}[X]$, viewed as a complex concentrated in degree $0$.

## Sources

- https://github.com/dagurtomas/LeanCondensed; D. Clausen and P. Scholze, lectures on analytic stacks and light condensed mathematics.; P. Scholze, Lectures on Condensed Mathematics, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.03658. Problem `derived_solidification_free_CW_homology` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Derived solidification is the left derived functor of solidification
articles.statement:
Let $Q$ denote the
localization functors from cochain complexes indexed by $\mathbb{Z}$ to derived categories.
Derived solidification, together with the comparison natural transformation from $Q$ followed by
derived solidification to degreewise solidification followed by $Q$, is a left derived functor of
the functor that applies solidification degreewise to a cochain complex of light condensed abelian
groups and then passes to the derived category of light solid abelian groups, with respect to the
quasi-isomorphisms of cochain complexes of light condensed abelian groups.

## Sources

- https://github.com/dagurtomas/LeanCondensed; D. Clausen and P. Scholze, lectures on analytic stacks and light condensed mathematics.; P. Scholze, Lectures on Condensed Mathematics, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.03658. Problem `derived_solidification_free_CW_homology` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Derived solidification
articles.statement:
A functor from the derived category of light condensed abelian
groups to the derived category of light solid abelian groups.

Separate statements require it to be the left derived functor of degreewise solidification and
left adjoint to the derived inclusion; these determine it up to natural isomorphism.

## Sources

- https://github.com/dagurtomas/LeanCondensed; D. Clausen and P. Scholze, lectures on analytic stacks and light condensed mathematics.; P. Scholze, Lectures on Condensed Mathematics, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.03658. Problem `derived_solidification_free_CW_homology` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Derived category of light condensed abelian groups
articles.statement:
The derived category of the abelian
category of light condensed abelian groups.

articles.title: Derived category of light solid abelian groups
articles.statement:
The derived category of the abelian
category of light solid abelian groups.

articles.title: Free light condensed abelian group functor on topological spaces
articles.statement:
The functor from
topological spaces to light condensed abelian groups sending a space $X$ to the free light
condensed abelian group $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ on the light condensed set associated with $X$.

articles.title: Free light condensed abelian group on a topological space
articles.statement:
For a topological space $X$,
$\mathbb{Z}[X]$ is the free light condensed abelian group on the light condensed set associated
with $X$.

articles.title: Degreewise inclusion of complexes of light solid abelian groups
articles.statement:
The functor from cochain
complexes indexed by $\mathbb{Z}$ of light solid abelian groups to cochain complexes indexed by
$\mathbb{Z}$ of light condensed abelian groups that applies the inclusion of light solid abelian
groups into light condensed abelian groups in each degree.

articles.title: Spaces admitting a CW complex structure
articles.statement:
A topological space $X$ has this property when
it admits a classical CW complex structure whose underlying set is all of $X$.

articles.title: The solidity class
articles.statement:
For a light condensed abelian group $A$, the class asserting that $A$
is solid.

articles.title: Solid light condensed abelian groups
articles.statement:
Write $\mathbb{Z}[S]$ for the free light condensed
abelian group on a light profinite set $S$, let $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ be the one-point
compactification of $\mathbb{N}$, and let
$P = \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]/\mathbb{Z}[\infty]$ be the cokernel of the map induced
by the inclusion of the point $\infty$. The shift $n \mapsto n + 1$, $\infty \mapsto \infty$
induces an endomorphism $1 - \mathrm{shift}$ of $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]$, and
hence of $P$. A light condensed abelian group $A$ is *solid* if precomposition with this
endomorphism of $P$ is an isomorphism from the internal hom $\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(P, A)$ to
itself.

articles.title: One minus shift on P
articles.statement:
Write $\mathbb{Z}[S]$ for the free light condensed abelian group on
a light profinite set $S$, let $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ be the one-point compactification of
$\mathbb{N}$, and let $P = \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]/\mathbb{Z}[\infty]$ be the
cokernel of the map induced by the inclusion of the point $\infty$. Let $\mathrm{shift}$ be the
endomorphism of $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]$ induced by $n \mapsto n + 1$,
$\infty \mapsto \infty$. The endomorphism $1 - \mathrm{shift}$ vanishes on $\mathbb{Z}[\infty]$,
so it factors through a morphism $P \to \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]$. Composing this
morphism with the projection onto $P$ gives the induced endomorphism $1 - \mathrm{shift}$ of
$P$.

articles.title: One minus shift on ℤ(ℕ ∪ {∞})
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]$ be the free
light condensed abelian group on the light profinite set $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, and let
$\mathrm{shift}$ be its endomorphism induced by the map $n \mapsto n + 1$, $\infty \mapsto \infty$.
This is the endomorphism $1 - \mathrm{shift}$ of $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]$.

articles.title: Maps out of P
articles.statement:
Write $\mathbb{Z}[S]$ for the free light condensed abelian group on a light
profinite set $S$, and let $P = \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]/\mathbb{Z}[\infty]$ be the
cokernel of the map $\mathbb{Z}[\infty] \to \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]$ induced by the
inclusion of the point $\infty$. Let $A$ be a light condensed abelian group and let
$f \colon \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}] \to A$ be a morphism whose composite with this
map is zero. Then $f$ factors through the projection
$\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}] \to P$, and this is the induced morphism $P \to A$.

articles.title: The map ℤ(∞) → ℤ(ℕ ∪ {∞})
articles.statement:
For a light profinite set $S$, let $\mathbb{Z}[S]$ be the free
light condensed abelian group on $S$, and let $\iota$ be the inclusion of the point $\infty$ into
$\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$. This is the morphism
$\mathbb{Z}[\infty] \to \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]$ induced by $\iota$, where
$\mathbb{Z}[\infty]$ is the free light condensed abelian group on a point.

articles.title: The projection onto P
articles.statement:
Write $\mathbb{Z}[S]$ for the free light condensed abelian group on
a light profinite set $S$, and let $P = \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]/\mathbb{Z}[\infty]$.
This is the quotient map $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}] \to P$, the cokernel projection
of the map $\mathbb{Z}[\infty] \to \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]$ induced by the
inclusion of the point $\infty$.

articles.title: P is a retract of ℤ(ℕ ∪ {∞})
articles.statement:
Write $\mathbb{Z}[S]$ for the free light condensed abelian
group on a light profinite set $S$. The quotient
$P = \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]/\mathbb{Z}[\infty]$ by the image of the map induced by
the inclusion of the point $\infty$ is a retract of $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]$: the
short exact sequence
$0 \to \mathbb{Z}[\infty] \to \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}] \to P \to 0$ splits, and a
section of the projection $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}] \to P$ from this splitting,
together with the projection, exhibits the retraction.

articles.title: The light condensed abelian group P
articles.statement:
For a light profinite set $S$, let $\mathbb{Z}[S]$ be
the free light condensed abelian group on $S$, and let $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ be the
one-point compactification of $\mathbb{N}$. Then
$P = \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]/\mathbb{Z}[\infty]$ is the cokernel of the morphism
$\mathbb{Z}[\infty] \to \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]$ induced by the inclusion of the
point $\infty$.

articles.title: Short exactness of the sequence defining $P$
articles.statement:
Write $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ for the
one-point compactification of $\mathbb{N}$, viewed as a light profinite set, and $\mathbb{Z}[S]$ for
the free light condensed abelian group on a light profinite set $S$, with $\mathbb{Z}[\infty]$ the
one on a point. The short complex of light condensed abelian groups
$\mathbb{Z}[\infty] \to \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}] \to P$, whose first map is induced
by the inclusion of the point $\infty$ and whose second map is the cokernel projection onto
$P = \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]/\mathbb{Z}[\infty]$, is short exact: the first map is
a monomorphism, the second map is an epimorphism, and the sequence is exact in the middle.

articles.title: A splitting of the sequence defining $P$
articles.statement:
Write $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ for the
one-point compactification of $\mathbb{N}$, viewed as a light profinite set, and $\mathbb{Z}[S]$ for
the free light condensed abelian group on a light profinite set $S$, with $\mathbb{Z}[\infty]$ the
one on a point. Let $f \colon \mathbb{Z}[\infty] \to \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]$ be
induced by the inclusion of the point $\infty$, and let
$g \colon \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}] \to P$ be the cokernel projection onto
$P = \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]/\mathbb{Z}[\infty]$. This is a chosen splitting of the
short exact sequence of light condensed abelian groups
$\mathbb{Z}[\infty] \xrightarrow{f} \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}] \xrightarrow{g} P$,
that is, maps $r \colon \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}] \to \mathbb{Z}[\infty]$ and
$s \colon P \to \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]$ such that $r \circ f = \mathrm{id}$,
$g \circ s = \mathrm{id}$ and $f \circ r + s \circ g = \mathrm{id}$, where $r$ is induced by the
map from $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ to the point.

articles.title: The short complex defining $P$
articles.statement:
Write $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ for the one-point
compactification of $\mathbb{N}$, viewed as a light profinite set, and $\mathbb{Z}[S]$ for the free
light condensed abelian group on a light profinite set $S$, with $\mathbb{Z}[\infty]$ the one on a
point. This is the short complex of light condensed abelian groups
$\mathbb{Z}[\infty] \to \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}] \to P$ whose first map is induced by
the inclusion of the point $\infty$ and whose second map is the cokernel projection onto
$P = \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]/\mathbb{Z}[\infty]$.

articles.title: The shift map on $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$
articles.statement:
Write $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ for the
one-point compactification of $\mathbb{N}$, viewed as a light profinite set. The shift map is the
continuous map $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\} \to \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ sending $n$ to $n + 1$
and $\infty$ to $\infty$.

articles.title: The singular chain complex as a complex of light condensed abelian groups
articles.statement:
This is the
functor from topological spaces to cochain complexes of light condensed abelian groups sending a
space $X$ to the complex whose term in degree $-n$, for $n \ge 0$, is the discrete light condensed
abelian group on the integral singular $n$-chains $C_n(X; \mathbb{Z})$, with the singular boundary
maps as differentials and zero in positive degrees.

articles.title: The singular chain functor on CW spaces
articles.statement:
This is the functor from the category of
topological spaces admitting a CW complex structure, with all continuous maps as morphisms, to the
derived category of light condensed abelian groups sending $X$ to its integral singular chain
complex, regarded as a cochain complex of discrete light condensed abelian groups with the
$n$-chains in degree $-n$.

articles.title: The singular chain functor into the derived category
articles.statement:
This is the functor from topological
spaces to the derived category of light condensed abelian groups sending a space $X$ to its
integral singular chain complex, regarded as a cochain complex of discrete light condensed abelian
groups with the $n$-chains in degree $-n$.

articles.title: The singular chains of a space in the derived category
articles.statement:
For a topological space $X$, this
is the integral singular chain complex of $X$, regarded as a cochain complex of discrete light
condensed abelian groups with the $n$-chains in degree $-n$, as an object of the derived category
of light condensed abelian groups.

articles.title: Singular homology as a light condensed abelian group
articles.statement:
For a topological space $X$ and
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, this is the discrete light condensed abelian group on the $n$-th integral
singular homology group $H_n(X; \mathbb{Z})$.

articles.title: The category of light solid abelian groups
articles.statement:
Write $\mathbb{Z}[S]$ for the free light
condensed abelian group on a light profinite set $S$, let $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ be the
one-point compactification of $\mathbb{N}$, viewed as a light profinite set, write $\mathrm{pt}$ for
the one-point light profinite set, and let $P$ be the cokernel of the map
$\mathbb{Z}[\mathrm{pt}] \to \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]$ induced by the inclusion of
the point $\infty$. The endomorphism $1 - \mathrm{shift}$ of
$\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}]$, where $\mathrm{shift}$ is induced by $n \mapsto n + 1$
and $\infty \mapsto \infty$, descends to an endomorphism of $P$. A light condensed abelian group
$A$ is solid when this endomorphism of $P$ induces an isomorphism of internal homs
$\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(P, A) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(P, A)$. The category of light solid
abelian groups is the full subcategory of light condensed abelian groups on the solid objects.

articles.title: Solidification adjunction
articles.statement:
An adjunction exhibiting the solidification functor from light
condensed abelian groups to light solid abelian groups as left adjoint to the inclusion of the full
subcategory of light solid abelian groups into light condensed abelian groups.

## Sources

- https://github.com/dagurtomas/LeanCondensed; D. Clausen and P. Scholze, lectures on analytic stacks and light condensed mathematics.; P. Scholze, Lectures on Condensed Mathematics, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.03658. Problem `derived_solidification_free_CW_homology` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Solidification
articles.statement:
The solidification functor from the category of light condensed abelian
groups to the category of light solid abelian groups.

This declaration fixes only the functor. Its intended characterization, as left adjoint to the
inclusion of light solid abelian groups into light condensed abelian groups, is the separate
solidification adjunction.

## Sources

- https://github.com/dagurtomas/LeanCondensed; D. Clausen and P. Scholze, lectures on analytic stacks and light condensed mathematics.; P. Scholze, Lectures on Condensed Mathematics, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.03658. Problem `derived_solidification_free_CW_homology` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Splitting of the inclusion of the point at infinity
articles.statement:
The inclusion of the point at infinity
into the one-point compactification $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ of $\mathbb{N}$ is a split
monomorphism of light profinite spaces, with retraction the unique map from
$\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ to the one-point space.

articles.title: Inclusion of CW spaces into topological spaces
articles.statement:
The inclusion functor from the full
subcategory of topological spaces admitting a classical CW complex structure into the category of
topological spaces.

articles.title: Inclusion of the point at infinity
articles.statement:
The morphism of light profinite spaces from the
one-point space to the one-point compactification $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ of $\mathbb{N}$
that sends the point to $\infty$.

articles.title: Eilenberg's theorem on compact convex absolute retracts
articles.statement:
(a) Every nonempty compact
convex subset of a complete metrizable locally convex topological vector space over
$\mathbb{R}$ is an absolute retract. (b) Every nonempty compact subset of a pseudometric
space that is convex in the sense of Wilson is an absolute retract.

The spaces in part (a) are the real Fréchet spaces, the spaces of type (B0).

## Sources

- S. Eilenberg, Problem 138 of the Scottish Book; the typescript heads the entry "Theorem; Eilenberg" and states both (a) and (b) as theorems. Part (a) is also the Dugundji theorem, see the 2026 survey "90+ years of the Scottish Book" (arXiv:2603.27867), which notes that every nonempty convex subset of a locally convex metrizable topological vector space is an absolute retract.

articles.title: Absolute retract
articles.statement:
A topological space $K$ is an absolute retract when $K$ is compact
and, for every separable metrizable space $X$ and every topological embedding
$e \colon K \to X$, there is a continuous map $r \colon X \to K$ with $r(e(k)) = k$ for all
$k \in K$.

articles.title: Wilson convexity
articles.statement:
A subset $K$ of a pseudometric space $X$ with distance $d$ is convex in
the sense of Wilson when for all $x, y \in K$ and every real $t$ with $0 \le t \le 1$ there is
exactly one $z \in K$ with $d(x, z) = t \, d(x, y)$ and $d(z, y) = (1 - t) \, d(x, y)$.

articles.title: Fixed point theorem for maps of compact convex sets
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 0$ and let $B$ be the
closed unit ball about the origin in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$. Let $f$ be a map from
subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ to subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ that sends every nonempty compact convex
subset of $B$ to a nonempty compact convex subset of $B$, and that is continuous in the Hausdorff
metric on the nonempty compact convex subsets of $B$. Then there is a nonempty compact convex set
$X_0 \subseteq B$ with $f(X_0) = X_0$.

This answers Ulam's Problem 42 of the Scottish Book, which asks this for closed convex sets inside
a ball $K$; inside a ball the closed convex sets are the compact ones, and the typescript's
"sphere $K$" is read as the solid ball. All sets are required to be nonempty, because the
Hausdorff distance used is degenerate at the empty set. The answer is yes: for $n \ge 2$ the space
of nonempty compact convex subsets of $B$ is homeomorphic to the Hilbert cube (Nadler, Quinn and
Stavrokas), which has the fixed-point property; for $n \le 1$ that space is a point or a $2$-cell,
and Brouwer's theorem applies.

## Sources

- S. Ulam, Problem 42 of the Scottish Book; S. B. Nadler, J. Quinn and N. Stavrokas, Pacific J. Math. 83 (1979), 441-462; the fixed-point theorem for the Hilbert cube; see the commentary in R. D. Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book, 2nd ed. (Birkhäuser, 2015).

articles.title: Hausdorff continuity on compact convex sets
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real normed space, let
$K \subseteq E$, let $f$ be a map from subsets of $E$ to subsets of $E$, and write $d_H$ for the
Hausdorff distance between subsets of $E$. Then $f$ is Hausdorff continuous on the compact convex
subsets of $K$ if for every nonempty compact convex set $X \subseteq K$ and every
$\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty compact convex set
$Y \subseteq K$ with $d_H(X, Y) < \delta$ satisfies $d_H(f(X), f(Y)) < \varepsilon$.

Here $d_H$ is taken to be $0$ where the Hausdorff distance is infinite, in particular when exactly
one of the two sets is empty. The values $f(X)$ are not required to be compact, convex or
nonempty.

articles.title: Hahn–Mazurkiewicz theorem
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a nonempty topological space that is compact,
connected, locally connected, Hausdorff and second countable. Then there is a continuous
surjection from the closed unit interval $[0,1]$ onto $X$.

## Sources

- H. Hahn, Jahresber. DMV 23 (1914); S. Mazurkiewicz, Fund. Math. 1 (1920) (announcement 1913); Willard, General Topology; Munkres, Topology 2nd ed., second-countable Hausdorff compact formulation.

articles.title: The Hilbert cube absorbs the letter T (Borsuk's Problem 175)
articles.statement:
Let $Q = [0,1]^{\mathbb{N}}$ be
the Hilbert cube and let $T \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be the letter-T curve. Both parts of Borsuk's
Problem 175 from the Scottish Book have affirmative answers: (a) the product $Q \times T$ is
homeomorphic to $Q$, and (b) the product $T^{\mathbb{N}}$ of countably many copies of $T$ is
homeomorphic to $Q$.

## Sources

- K. Borsuk, Problem 175 of the Scottish Book; positively solved by R. D. Anderson, as cited in Domoradzki-Stawiska-Zarichnyi, "90+ years of the Scottish Book" (arXiv:2603.27867), and in the commentary in R. D. Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book, 2nd ed. (Birkhäuser, 2015).

articles.title: The Hilbert cube
articles.statement:
The Hilbert cube $Q = [0,1]^{\mathbb{N}}$ is the product of countably
many copies of the closed unit interval $[0,1]$, with the product topology.

articles.title: The letter T
articles.statement:
The letter-T curve is the subset

$$T = \{(0, y) : 0 \le y \le 1\} \cup \{(x, 1) : -1 \le x \le 1\}$$

of $\mathbb{R}^2$: a vertical stem with a horizontal bar on top, meeting at the branch point
$(0, 1)$.

articles.title: Peano's space-filling curve
articles.statement:
There exists a continuous surjection from the closed unit interval to its square.

## Sources

- G. Peano, "Sur une courbe, qui remplit toute une aire plane", Mathematische Annalen 36 (1890), 157-160.

articles.title: Path-connected nonseparating plane continua have the fixed point property
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a
nonempty, compact, path-connected subset of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose complement
$\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus K$ is connected. Then $K$ has the fixed point property: every continuous
map $f \colon K \to K$ has a point $x \in K$ with $f(x) = x$.

This answers the nonseparating planar continuum conjecture in the affirmative. Hagopian (A
fixed-point theorem for plane continua, Bull. AMS 77 (1971), 351-354; addendum 1972) proved that
every arcwise connected nonseparating plane continuum has the fixed point property, and compact
path-connected subsets of the plane are arcwise connected.

## Sources

- A. M. Blokh, R. J. Fokkink, J. C. Mayer, L. G. Oversteegen, E. D. Tymchatyn, Fixed point theorems for plane continua with applications, Mem. Amer. Math. Soc. 224 (2013), no. 1053, arXiv:1004.0214 (citing C. L. Hagopian, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 77 (1971), 351-354), https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.0214.

articles.title: Nonseparating planar continuum conjecture
articles.statement:
The conjecture asserts that every nonempty,
compact, path-connected subset $K$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose complement
$\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus K$ is connected (that is, $K$ does not separate the plane) has the fixed
point property: every continuous map $f \colon K \to K$ has a point $x \in K$ with $f(x) = x$.

## Sources

- Open Problem Garden, node ID 37295, http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/nonseparating_planar_continuum.

articles.title: Fixed point property
articles.statement:
A subset $K$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ has the fixed
point property when every continuous map $f \colon K \to K$ has a fixed point, that is, a point
$x \in K$ with $f(x) = x$.

## Sources

- Open Problem Garden, node ID 37295, http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/nonseparating_planar_continuum.

articles.title: Unit spheres of infinite-dimensional Banach spaces are unicoherent
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real
Banach space that is not finite-dimensional, and let $S = \{x \in E : \|x\| = 1\}$ be its unit
sphere. If $A$ and $B$ are closed connected subsets of $S$ with $A \cup B = S$, then $A \cap B$ is
connected. Here connected sets are nonempty by definition.

This answers Banach's Problem 46 of the Scottish Book: is the sphere in a space of type (B)
uni-coherent, that is, whenever it is the union of two continua $A$ and $B$, is $A \cap B$
connected? Continua are read as closed connected sets, the meaning of uni-coherence for
non-compact spaces: in infinite dimensions the sphere is not compact, so two compact sets could
not cover it. The statement is restricted to infinite-dimensional spaces; in dimension $1$ the
sphere is two points and in dimension $2$ it is a circle, and neither is uni-coherent (two
semicircles cover the circle and meet in two points). In infinite dimensions the sphere is an
absolute retract, and the affirmative answer follows from the theorems of Borsuk and Eilenberg
recorded in the addendum.

## Sources

- S. Banach, Problem 46 of the Scottish Book; addendum in the Scottish Book citing Borsuk and Eilenberg, Fund. Math. 26, p. 61; see the commentary in R. D. Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book, 2nd ed. (Birkhäuser, 2015).

articles.title: Scottish Book Problem 7 fails: closed convex sets need not be homeomorphic
articles.statement:
The Scottish Book
Problem 7 claim is false: there are a real Banach space $E$ and closed convex subsets
$A, B \subseteq E$, each with infinite-dimensional linear span, that are not homeomorphic.

For example, a compact infinite-dimensional closed convex set, such as the Hilbert cube, is not
homeomorphic to a noncompact one, such as the whole space, since compactness is a topological
invariant.

## Sources

- S. Mazur and S. Banach, Problem 7 of the Scottish Book; T. Banakh's observation as reported in the 2026 survey "90+ years of the Scottish Book" (arXiv:2603.27867). The modified classification problem was solved for Frechet spaces by Banakh-Cauty, Studia Mathematica 205 (2011) 1-11.

articles.title: Retraction onto the unit sphere of Hilbert space
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be an infinite-dimensional real
Hilbert space and let $S = \{x \in E : \|x\| = 1\}$ be its unit sphere. Then there is a
continuous map $f : E \to E$ such that $f(x) \in S$ for every $x \in E$ and $f(x) = x$ for every
$x \in S$.

Restricting $f$ to the closed unit ball gives a retraction of the ball onto $S$; conversely, a
retraction $r$ of the closed unit ball onto $S$ extends to all of $E$ by
$f(x) = r(x / \max(1, \|x\|))$. In finite dimensions no such map exists, by the Brouwer
no-retraction theorem, so the infinite-dimensional hypothesis is essential.

## Sources

- S. Ulam, Problem 36 of the Scottish Book, asking whether there is a retraction of the closed unit ball of Hilbert space onto its boundary; the answer is affirmative, see the commentary in R. D. Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book, 2nd ed. (Birkhäuser, 2015), and the 2026 survey "90+ years of the Scottish Book" (arXiv:2603.27867), which notes that the unit sphere of a Hilbert space is homeomorphic to the whole space.

articles.title: Projective Hilbert space homeomorphic to the space itself
articles.statement:
For a real inner product
space $E$, the statement that the projective Hilbert space of $E$, the unit sphere
$\{x \in E : \|x\| = 1\}$ with each $x$ identified with $-x$ and given the quotient topology,
is homeomorphic to $E$.

articles.title: Projective Hilbert space is not homeomorphic to Hilbert space
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be an
infinite-dimensional real Hilbert space. Then the projective Hilbert space of $E$, the unit
sphere $\{x \in E : \|x\| = 1\}$ with each $x$ identified with $-x$ and given the quotient
topology, is not homeomorphic to $E$.

This answers Ulam's Problem 35 of the Scottish Book in the negative. The projective space is the
standard model of the space of diameters of the unit sphere with the Hausdorff metric. Hilbert
space is contractible, hence simply connected, while projective Hilbert space is not, its
fundamental group being $\mathbb{Z}/2$ via the double covering by the unit sphere.

## Sources

- S. Ulam, Problem 35 of the Scottish Book; see the commentary of Holsztynski in R. D. Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book, 2nd ed. (Birkhäuser, 2015), and the Hilbert-manifold classification by homotopy type.

articles.title: Projective Hilbert space
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed additive commutative group, in practice a
real inner product space. The projective Hilbert space of $E$ is the quotient of the unit sphere
$\{x \in E : \|x\| = 1\}$ by the relation identifying each $x$ with $-x$. Its points are the
antipodal pairs $\{x, -x\}$ of unit vectors, that is, the diameters of the unit sphere.

When $E$ is a real inner product space, it carries the quotient topology of the unit sphere.

articles.title: Scottish Book Problem 7 (Mazur–Banach)
articles.statement:
The claim that in every real Banach space $E$,
any two closed convex subsets $A, B \subseteq E$ whose linear spans are infinite-dimensional are
homeomorphic, with the subspace topologies.

articles.title: Scottish Book Problem 167
articles.statement:
Ulam's claim that for every infinite-dimensional real Hilbert
space $H$ with unit sphere $S = \{p \in H : \|p\| = 1\}$, every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, all
continuous functions $f_1, \dots, f_n : S \to \mathbb{R}$ and every continuous map
$T : S \to S$, there is a point $p_0 \in S$ with $f_i(T(p_0)) = f_i(p_0)$ for every $i$.

articles.title: Negative answer to Scottish Book Problem 167
articles.statement:
Ulam's claim in Problem 167 is false: there
are an infinite-dimensional real Hilbert space $H$ with unit sphere $S$, a number
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, continuous functions $f_1, \dots, f_n : S \to \mathbb{R}$ and a continuous map
$T : S \to S$ such that no point $p_0 \in S$ satisfies $f_i(T(p_0)) = f_i(p_0)$ for every $i$.

The claim fails already for one function.

## Sources

- S. Ulam, Problem 167 of the Scottish Book; refuted via V. Klee's homeomorphism of the Hilbert sphere onto the whole Hilbert space: composing that homeomorphism with a translation gives a continuous `T` and a continuous `f` with no point `p0` satisfying `f (T p0) = f p0`. See the commentary in R. D. Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book, 2nd ed. (Birkhäuser, 2015).

articles.title: Alexandrov–Urysohn theorem on Baire space
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a nonempty Polish space that
is zero-dimensional (for every point $x$ and every open set $U$ containing $x$ there is a clopen
set $V$ with $x \in V \subseteq U$) and in which every compact subset has empty interior. Then $X$
is homeomorphic to the Baire space $\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$ of all sequences of natural numbers,
with the product of the discrete topologies.

## Sources

- Alexandrov–Urysohn characterization; A. S. Kechris, Classical Descriptive Set Theory (1995), Theorem 7.7.

articles.title: Zero-dimensional space
articles.statement:
A topological space $X$ is zero-dimensional if for every point
$x \in X$ and every open set $U \subseteq X$ containing $x$ there is a clopen set $V$ with
$x \in V \subseteq U$.

articles.title: Winning strategy for the first player in the Banach–Mazur game
articles.statement:
Let
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. In this game a move is a pair of reals $(c, d)$, standing for the open
interval $(c, d)$, and a valid strategy is a map from pairs to pairs answering each pair $(c, d)$
with $c < d$ by a pair $(c', d')$ with $c \le c' < d' \le d$. Player A has a winning strategy for
$E$ if there are reals $a < b$ and a valid strategy $\sigma_A$ such that, for every valid strategy
$\sigma_B$, the play $(c_n, d_n)_{n \ge 0}$ given by $(c_0, d_0) = (a, b)$,
$(c_{n+1}, d_{n+1}) = \sigma_B(c_n, d_n)$ for even $n$ and
$(c_{n+1}, d_{n+1}) = \sigma_A(c_n, d_n)$ for odd $n$ satisfies
$\left(\bigcap_{n} (c_n, d_n)\right) \cap E \neq \emptyset$.

articles.title: Winning strategy for the second player in the Banach–Mazur game
articles.statement:
Let
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. In this game a move is a pair of reals $(c, d)$, standing for the open
interval $(c, d)$, and a valid strategy is a map from pairs to pairs answering each pair $(c, d)$
with $c < d$ by a pair $(c', d')$ with $c \le c' < d' \le d$. Player B has a winning strategy for
$E$ if there is a valid strategy $\sigma_B$ such that, for all reals $a < b$ and every valid
strategy $\sigma_A$, the play $(c_n, d_n)_{n \ge 0}$ given by $(c_0, d_0) = (a, b)$,
$(c_{n+1}, d_{n+1}) = \sigma_B(c_n, d_n)$ for even $n$ and
$(c_{n+1}, d_{n+1}) = \sigma_A(c_n, d_n)$ for odd $n$ satisfies
$\left(\bigcap_{n} (c_n, d_n)\right) \cap E = \emptyset$.

articles.title: Plays of the Banach–Mazur game
articles.statement:
Let $(a, b)$ be a pair of reals and let $\sigma_A$ and
$\sigma_B$ be strategies for A and B, maps from pairs of reals to pairs of reals. A sequence
$(p_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of pairs of reals is the play that opens with $(a, b)$ and follows $\sigma_A$
and $\sigma_B$ if $p_0 = (a, b)$, $p_{n+1} = \sigma_B(p_n)$ for every even $n$, and
$p_{n+1} = \sigma_A(p_n)$ for every odd $n$: A opens at index $0$ and moves at the other even
indices, B moves at the odd indices.

articles.title: Valid strategies in the Banach–Mazur game
articles.statement:
A strategy in the Banach–Mazur game is a map
$\sigma \colon \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$, a pair $(a, b)$
standing for the open interval $(a, b)$. It is valid if for all reals $a < b$ the pair
$(c, d) = \sigma(a, b)$ satisfies $a \le c < d \le b$, so that it answers each nonempty open
interval with a nonempty open subinterval, possibly the interval itself. Nothing is required of
$\sigma$ on pairs $(a, b)$ with $a \ge b$.

Strategies are taken to depend only on the opponent's last move: the rest of the game depends
only on the current interval.

articles.title: Banach–Mazur game theorem
articles.statement:
For every set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, player A has a winning
strategy in the Banach–Mazur game for $E$ if and only if there are reals $a < b$ such that
$(a, b) \setminus E$ is meagre, and player B has a winning strategy in the Banach–Mazur game for
$E$ if and only if $E$ is meagre.

This answers Mazur's Problem 43 of the Scottish Book. Given $E$, A picks an interval $d_1$,
B picks a subinterval $d_2$ of $d_1$, A picks a subinterval $d_3$ of $d_2$, and so on; A wins if
the intersection of all the chosen intervals meets $E$. Mazur asked whether A has a winning
method only when the complement of $E$ is of first category in some interval, and whether B has
one when $E$ is of first category. Both answers are affirmative, in the characterization form
above (Oxtoby).

## Sources

- S. Mazur, Problem 43 of the Scottish Book; addendum of S. Banach, 4 August 1935: "Mazur's conjecture is true"; J. C. Oxtoby, The Banach-Mazur game and Banach category theorem; see the commentary in R. D. Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book, 2nd ed. (Birkhäuser, 2015).

articles.title: Existence of a Bernstein set
articles.statement:
There is a set $B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ such that every closed,
uncountable set $F \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ meets both $B$ and its complement $\mathbb{R} \setminus B$.

## Sources

- F. Bernstein (construction); J. C. Oxtoby, Measure and Category, 2nd ed. (1980); A. S. Kechris, Classical Descriptive Set Theory, Thm 8.24 (1995).

articles.title: Everywhere differentiable functions do not form a Borel set
articles.statement:
In the space $C((0, 1))$ of
continuous real functions on the open interval $(0, 1)$, with the compact-open topology (uniform
convergence on compact subsets), the set of functions that have a derivative at every point of
$(0, 1)$ is not a Borel set.

This is Banach's Problem 52 of the Scottish Book. The typescript also records that this class is
not an $F_\sigma$ set, that it is coanalytic, and that the problem was solved by Mazurkiewicz.

## Sources

- S. Banach, Problem 52 of the Scottish Book; solved by Mazurkiewicz, as recorded in typescript Ad 52; see the commentary in R. D. Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book, 2nd ed. (Birkhäuser, 2015).

articles.title: Functions differentiable at every point of $(0, 1)$
articles.statement:
A continuous function
$f \colon (0, 1) \to \mathbb{R}$ has a derivative at every point if for every $x \in (0, 1)$ the
function $\tilde f \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ equal to $f$ on $(0, 1)$ and to $0$ outside
$(0, 1)$ is differentiable at $x$. Since $\tilde f$ agrees with $f$ near every point of $(0, 1)$,
this depends only on $f$: it says that $f$ is differentiable at every point of $(0, 1)$.

articles.title: Brouwer's characterization of the Cantor space
articles.statement:
Every nonempty compact metrizable perfect totally disconnected space is homeomorphic to the Cantor
space.

## Sources

- L. E. J. Brouwer, Proc. Kon. Ned. Akad. Wet. 12 (1910), 785-794.

articles.title: Sierpinski's characterization of the rationals
articles.statement:
Every nonempty countable metrizable space with no isolated points is homeomorphic to Q.

## Sources

- W. Sierpinski, Sur une propriete topologique, Fund. Math. 1 (1920), 11-16, DOI 10.4064/FM-1-1-11-16.

articles.title: Covering dimension at most n
articles.statement:
A topological space $X$ has covering dimension at most
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ if every finite open cover $U_1, \dots, U_m$ of $X$ has a finite open
refinement $V_1, \dots, V_k$ (open sets covering $X$, each contained in some $U_i$) in which any
$n + 2$ members with distinct indices have empty intersection, that is, the refinement has order
at most $n + 1$.

articles.title: Small inductive and covering dimension can differ for compact Hausdorff spaces
articles.statement:
Scottish
Book Problem 187, part (2), has a negative answer: it is not the case that for every compact
Hausdorff space $X$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X$ has small inductive dimension at most $n$
if and only if $X$ has covering dimension at most $n$.

The small inductive dimension is used here; Alexandroff's typescript does not say whether small or
large inductive dimension is meant. The Lunts–Lokutsievskii example is a compact Hausdorff space
$X$ whose covering dimension $\dim X$ differs from its small inductive dimension
$\operatorname{ind} X$ (Encyclopedia of Mathematics, "Dimension theory"; R. Engelking, Dimension
Theory, North-Holland, 1978).

## Sources

- P. Alexandroff, Problem 187 part (2) of the Scottish Book, typescript pp. 82–83.

articles.title: The p-dimensional cube
articles.statement:
For $p \in \mathbb{N}$, the cube $I^p = [0,1]^p$ is the set of
points of $\mathbb{R}^p$ all of whose coordinates lie in $[0,1]$, with the subspace topology.

articles.title: Kolmogorov's open map raising dimension
articles.statement:
An interior (open) mapping can raise dimension:
there are compact metrizable spaces $X$ and $Y$, where $X$ has small inductive dimension exactly
$1$ and $Y$ has small inductive dimension exactly $2$, and a continuous open surjective map
$f \colon X \to Y$. A space has small inductive dimension exactly $n$ when its small inductive
dimension is at most $n$ but not at most $n - 1$.

## Sources

- S. Eilenberg, Problem 136 of the Scottish Book, asking whether an interior mapping can increase dimension; answered affirmatively by A. Kolmogorov, Annals of Mathematics 38 (1937), pp. 34-38, who gave an example of a continuous interior mapping raising dimension from 1 to 2, as recorded in the typescript Ad 136.

articles.title: Open maps can raise the dimension of a cube
articles.statement:
There are natural numbers $p < q$ and a
continuous, open, surjective map $f \colon I^p \to I^q$, where $I^p = [0,1]^p$ and
$I^q = [0,1]^q$ are the $p$- and $q$-dimensional cubes.

Keldysh constructed such maps, refuting the claim of Scottish Book Problem 187, part (3), that no
open (interior) continuous map of a $p$-dimensional cube onto a $q$-dimensional cube exists for
$p < q$.

## Sources

- P. Alexandroff, Problem 187 part (3) of the Scottish Book, typescript pp. 82–83; see the commentary in R. D. Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book, 2nd ed. (Birkhäuser, 2015).

articles.title: Direct limit equivalence relation
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in I}$ be a family of topological
spaces indexed by a preorder $I$, with maps $f_{ij} : X_i \to X_j$ for $i \le j$ forming a
directed system. This is the smallest equivalence relation on the disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_{i \in I} X_i$ that relates $(i, x)$ to $(j, f_{ij}(x))$ for all $i \le j$ and
$x \in X_i$.

articles.title: The induced map out of the direct limit is continuous
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in I}$ be a
directed system of topological spaces over a preorder $I$ with continuous transition maps
$f_{ij} : X_i \to X_j$, and let $Y$ be a topological space. If the maps
$\psi_i : X_i \to Y$ are continuous and satisfy $\psi_j(f_{ij}(x)) = \psi_i(x)$ for all
$i \le j$ and $x \in X_i$, then the induced map $\varinjlim X_i \to Y$ from the direct limit,
sending the class of $(i, x)$ to $\psi_i(x)$, is continuous.

articles.title: Map out of the direct limit
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in I}$ be a directed system of
topological spaces over a preorder $I$ with continuous transition maps
$f_{ij} : X_i \to X_j$, and let $Y$ be a topological space. A family of maps
$\psi_i : X_i \to Y$ with $\psi_j(f_{ij}(x)) = \psi_i(x)$ for all $i \le j$ and $x \in X_i$
induces the map $\varinjlim X_i \to Y$ from the direct limit that sends the class of $(i, x)$
to $\psi_i(x)$.

articles.title: Canonical maps commute with the transition maps
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in I}$ be a directed
system of topological spaces over a preorder $I$ with continuous transition maps
$f_{ij} : X_i \to X_j$. The canonical maps $\iota_i : X_i \to \varinjlim X_i$ into the direct
limit satisfy $\iota_j(f_{ij}(x)) = \iota_i(x)$ for all $i \le j$ and $x \in X_i$.

articles.title: Canonical maps into the direct limit are continuous
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in I}$ be a
directed system of topological spaces over a preorder $I$ with continuous transition maps
$f_{ij} : X_i \to X_j$. For every $i \in I$, the canonical map
$\iota_i : X_i \to \varinjlim X_i$ into the direct limit is continuous.

articles.title: Canonical map into the direct limit
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in I}$ be a directed system of
topological spaces over a preorder $I$ with continuous transition maps
$f_{ij} : X_i \to X_j$. For $i \in I$, the canonical map $\iota_i : X_i \to \varinjlim X_i$
into the direct limit sends $x$ to the class of $(i, x)$.

articles.title: Generating relation of a direct limit
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in I}$ be a family of
topological spaces indexed by a preorder $I$, with maps $f_{ij} : X_i \to X_j$ for $i \le j$
forming a directed system ($f_{ii}$ is the identity and $f_{jk} \circ f_{ij} = f_{ik}$ for
$i \le j \le k$). This relation on the disjoint union $\bigsqcup_{i \in I} X_i$ relates
$(i, x)$ to $(j, f_{ij}(x))$ for all $i \le j$ and $x \in X_i$, and relates no other pairs.

articles.title: Direct limit of topological spaces
articles.statement:
Let $I$ be a preorder, $(X_i)_{i \in I}$ a family
of topological spaces, and $f_{ij} : X_i \to X_j$ for $i \le j$ continuous maps forming a
directed system ($f_{ii}$ is the identity and $f_{jk} \circ f_{ij} = f_{ik}$ for
$i \le j \le k$). The direct limit $\varinjlim X_i$ is the quotient of the disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_{i \in I} X_i$ by the equivalence relation generated by $(i, x) \sim (j, f_{ij}(x))$
for $i \le j$ and $x \in X_i$, with the quotient topology of the disjoint union topology.

The directed-system laws and the continuity of the transition maps are hypotheses of the
construction: the underlying quotient does not use them, but without them it need not be a
direct limit of topological spaces.

articles.title: Bounded metric $d/(1+d)$ is equivalent to $d$
articles.statement:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and define

\[
\delta(x,y):=\frac{d(x,y)}{1+d(x,y)}, \qquad x,y\in X.
\]
Prove that $d$ and $\delta$ are equivalent metrics on $X$.

Lean variant: the source statement asserts only that `d`-balls and `δ`-balls are mutually nested,
which omits the claim that `δ` is a metric; the metric axioms of `δ` are added as a first conjunct.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Inequalities in real analysis), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_65`, with the change above.

articles.title: Homogeneous topological space
articles.statement: A topological space is homogeneous if its homeomorphism group acts transitively.

articles.title: A preconnected set meets the frontier of every set it crosses
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a
preconnected subset of a topological space $X$ and let $A \subseteq X$. If both $s \cap A$ and
$s \cap (X \setminus A)$ are nonempty, then $s$ meets the frontier
$\partial A = \overline{A} \setminus \operatorname{int} A$ of $A$, that is,
$s \cap \partial A$ is nonempty.

articles.title: Inverse limit as compatible tuples
articles.statement:
Let $I$ be a preordered set, let $(X_i)_{i \in I}$
be a family of sets, and for every $i \le j$ let $f_{ij} \colon X_j \to X_i$ be a map. The inverse
limit is the set of tuples $x = (x_i)_{i \in I}$ in the product $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ such that
$f_{ij}(x_j) = x_i$ whenever $i \le j$.

## Sources

- ATLAS NumberTheoryI, Definition 8.9.

articles.title: The inverse limit is closed
articles.statement:
Let $I$ be a preordered set, let $(X_i)_{i \in I}$ be a
family of Hausdorff topological spaces, and for every $i \le j$ let $f_{ij} \colon X_j \to X_i$
be a continuous map. Then the inverse limit
$\{x \in \prod_{i \in I} X_i : f_{ij}(x_j) = x_i \text{ for all } i \le j\}$ is closed in the
product $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$.

Each equation $f_{ij}(x_j) = x_i$ cuts out a closed set because $X_i$ is Hausdorff, and the
limit is the intersection of all of them.

articles.title: The inverse limit of compact Hausdorff spaces is compact
articles.statement:
Let $I$ be a preordered set, let
$(X_i)_{i \in I}$ be a family of compact Hausdorff topological spaces, and for every $i \le j$
let $f_{ij} \colon X_j \to X_i$ be a continuous map. Then the inverse limit
$\{x \in \prod_{i \in I} X_i : f_{ij}(x_j) = x_i \text{ for all } i \le j\}$ is compact in the
product $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$.

It is a closed subset of a compact product.

articles.title: Membership in the inverse limit
articles.statement:
Let $I$ be a preordered set, let $(X_i)_{i \in I}$ be a
family of sets, and for every $i \le j$ let $f_{ij} \colon X_j \to X_i$ be a map. A tuple
$x \in \prod_{i \in I} X_i$ lies in the inverse limit if and only if $f_{ij}(x_j) = x_i$ for all
$i \le j$.

articles.title: Elements of the inverse limit are compatible
articles.statement:
Let $I$ be a preordered set, let
$(X_i)_{i \in I}$ be a family of sets, and for every $i \le j$ let $f_{ij} \colon X_j \to X_i$ be
a map. If $x = (x_i)_{i \in I}$ lies in the inverse limit, then $f_{ij}(x_j) = x_i$ for all
$i \le j$.

articles.title: Non-strictly separated sets
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a pseudo-extended metric space (distances lie in
$[0, \infty]$ and distinct points may be at distance $0$), write $d$ for its extended distance,
and let $\varepsilon \in [0, \infty]$. A set $s \subseteq X$ is $\varepsilon$-separated if
$\varepsilon \le d(x, y)$ for all distinct points $x, y \in s$.

articles.title: Kuratowski's closure-complement theorem
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a topological space and $s \subseteq X$.
The sets that can be obtained from $s$ by applying closure and complement finitely many times
(including $s$ itself) form a finite family of at most $14$ distinct sets.

## Sources

- Casimir Kuratowski, "Sur l'opération Ā de l'Analysis Situs," *Fundamenta Mathematicae* 3 (1922), 182–199, DOI 10.4064/FM-3-1-182-199.

articles.title: Countably monolithic space
articles.statement:
A topological space is countably monolithic (ω-monolithic) if the closure
of every countable subspace has a countable network.

articles.title: Second-countable spaces have a countable network
articles.statement:
Every second-countable topological
space has a countable network.

articles.title: Countable network
articles.statement:
A topological space $X$ has a countable network if there is a
countable family $\mathcal{N}$ of subsets of $X$ such that for every open set $U \subseteq X$
and every point $x \in U$ there is some $V \in \mathcal{N}$ with $x \in V \subseteq U$.

Network sets need not themselves be open.

articles.title: The cofinite filter lies below the principal filter of the complement of a finite set
articles.statement:
For every finite set $S$ of indices in $\iota$, the cofinite filter on $\iota$ is less than or
equal to the principal filter of the complement $\iota \setminus S$; that is, $\iota \setminus S$
belongs to the cofinite filter.

articles.title: Continuity of the map from the direct limit of the pieces
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be
topological spaces with subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$, and for a finite set $S \subseteq \iota$ let
$X_S$ be the set of tuples $x \in \prod_i X_i$ with $x_i \in U_i$ for all $i \notin S$, with the
subspace topology of the product topology. The map from the direct limit $\varinjlim_S X_S$ over
the finite subsets of $\iota$ to the restricted product $\prod'_i (X_i, U_i)$ (with respect to the
cofinite filter, with its restricted product topology) that sends the class of $x \in X_S$ to $x$
is continuous.

This follows from the universal property of the direct limit.

articles.title: Continuity of the inclusion of pieces
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be topological spaces with
subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$, and for a finite set $S \subseteq \iota$ let $X_S$ be the set of
tuples $x \in \prod_i X_i$ with $x_i \in U_i$ for all $i \notin S$, with the subspace topology of
the product topology. For finite sets $S \subseteq T \subseteq \iota$, the inclusion map
$X_S \to X_T$ is continuous.

articles.title: Continuity of the chunk map
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be topological spaces with subsets
$U_i \subseteq X_i$, let $S \subseteq \iota$ be finite, and let $X_S$ be the set of tuples
$x \in \prod_i X_i$ with $x_i \in U_i$ for all $i \notin S$, with the subspace topology of the
product topology. The map that sends $x \in X_S$ to $x$, viewed in the restricted product of the
$(X_i, U_i)$ with respect to the principal filter of $\iota \setminus S$ with its restricted
product topology, is continuous.

articles.title: Continuity of the map to the direct limit of the pieces
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be
topological spaces with subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$, and for a finite set $S \subseteq \iota$ let
$X_S$ be the set of tuples $x \in \prod_i X_i$ with $x_i \in U_i$ for all $i \notin S$, with the
subspace topology of the product topology. The map from the restricted product
$\prod'_i (X_i, U_i)$ (with respect to the cofinite filter, with its restricted product topology)
to the direct limit $\varinjlim_S X_S$ over the finite subsets of $\iota$ that sends $x$ to its
class in $X_{S(x)}$, where $S(x)$ is the finite set of indices $i$ with $x_i \notin U_i$, is
continuous.

This follows from the universal property of the restricted product topology.

articles.title: Continuity of the transition maps of the pieces
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be topological
spaces with subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$, and for a finite set $S \subseteq \iota$ let $X_S$ be the
set of tuples $x \in \prod_i X_i$ with $x_i \in U_i$ for all $i \notin S$, with the subspace
topology of the product topology. For all finite sets $S \subseteq T \subseteq \iota$, the
transition map $X_S \to X_T$ of the direct system of the pieces, which is the inclusion, is
continuous.

articles.title: Direct limit of the finite-support pieces
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be topological spaces
with subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$, and for a finite set $S \subseteq \iota$ let $X_S$ be the set of
tuples $x \in \prod_i X_i$ with $x_i \in U_i$ for all $i \notin S$, with the subspace topology of
the product topology. The space $\varinjlim_S X_S$ is the direct limit of the $X_S$ over the
finite subsets $S$ of $\iota$ ordered by inclusion, with the inclusions $X_S \to X_T$ for
$S \subseteq T$ as transition maps: the quotient of the disjoint union of the $X_S$ by the
equivalence relation generated by identifying each $x \in X_S$ with its image in $X_T$, with the
quotient topology.

articles.title: The backward map undoes the forward map
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be topological spaces
with subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$, and for a finite set $S \subseteq \iota$ let $X_S$ be the set of
tuples $x \in \prod_i X_i$ with $x_i \in U_i$ for all $i \notin S$. For every $x$ in the
restricted product $\prod'_i (X_i, U_i)$ with respect to the cofinite filter, let $S(x)$ be the
finite set of indices $i$ with $x_i \notin U_i$. Sending $x$ to its class in $X_{S(x)}$ in the
direct limit $\varinjlim_S X_S$, and then sending that class to the tuple carried by its
representative, returns $x$.

This holds definitionally: unfolding both maps, the quotient lift applied to the canonical
representative returns the representative itself.

articles.title: The map from the direct limit of the pieces to the restricted product
articles.statement:
Let
$(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be topological spaces with subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$, and for a finite set
$S \subseteq \iota$ let $X_S$ be the set of tuples $x \in \prod_i X_i$ with $x_i \in U_i$ for all
$i \notin S$, with the subspace topology of the product topology. The backward map sends the class
in the direct limit $\varinjlim_S X_S$ (over the finite subsets of $\iota$) of a tuple
$x \in X_S$ to $x$, regarded as an element of the restricted product $\prod'_i (X_i, U_i)$ with
respect to the cofinite filter; the result does not depend on the representative.

articles.title: The restricted product is the direct limit of its finite-support pieces
articles.statement:
Let
$(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be topological spaces with subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$, and for a finite set
$S \subseteq \iota$ let $X_S$ be the set of tuples $x \in \prod_i X_i$ with $x_i \in U_i$ for all
$i \notin S$, with the subspace topology of the product topology. Let $\prod'_i (X_i, U_i)$ be
the restricted product with respect to the cofinite filter, with its restricted product
topology, and for $x$ in it let $S(x)$ be the finite set of indices $i$ with $x_i \notin U_i$.
The map sending $x$ to its class in $X_{S(x)}$ is a homeomorphism from $\prod'_i (X_i, U_i)$ to
the direct limit $\varinjlim_S X_S$ over the finite subsets of $\iota$ ordered by inclusion; its
inverse sends the class of $x \in X_S$ to $x$.

## Sources

- ATLAS NumberTheoryI, Proposition 25.5.

articles.title: Inclusion of pieces
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be topological spaces with subsets
$U_i \subseteq X_i$, and for a finite set $S \subseteq \iota$ let $X_S$ be the set of tuples
$x \in \prod_i X_i$ with $x_i \in U_i$ for all $i \notin S$. For finite sets $S \subseteq T$, the
inclusion of pieces is the map $X_S \to X_T$ sending each tuple $x$ to itself.

articles.title: Tuples restricted on a cofinite set lie in a piece
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be sets
with subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$, and for a finite set $F \subseteq \iota$ let $X_F$ be the set
of tuples $x \in \prod_i X_i$ with $x_i \in U_i$ for all $i \notin F$. Let $S \subseteq \iota$
have finite complement. Then every tuple $y \in \prod_i X_i$ with $y_i \in U_i$ for all
$i \in S$ lies in $X_{\iota \setminus S}$.

articles.title: Every element of the restricted product lies in a piece
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be
sets with subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$, and let $x$ be an element of the restricted product of
the $X_i$ with respect to the $U_i$, that is, a tuple $x \in \prod_i X_i$ with $x_i \in U_i$ for
all but finitely many $i$. Then there is a finite set $S \subseteq \iota$ such that
$x_i \in U_i$ for all $i \notin S$, that is, $x$ lies in the piece $X_S$.

articles.title: An element lies in the piece indexed by its support
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be sets
with subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$, let $x$ be an element of the restricted product of the $X_i$
with respect to the $U_i$ (a tuple with $x_i \in U_i$ for all but finitely many $i$), and let
$\operatorname{supp}(x)$ be the finite set of indices $i$ with $x_i \notin U_i$. Then
$x_i \in U_i$ for every $i \notin \operatorname{supp}(x)$, that is, $x$ lies in the piece
$X_{\operatorname{supp}(x)}$.

articles.title: The support lies in the index set of every piece containing the element
articles.statement:
Let
$(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be sets with subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$, and let $x$ be an element of the
restricted product of the $X_i$ with respect to the $U_i$ (a tuple with $x_i \in U_i$ for all but
finitely many $i$), with support $\operatorname{supp}(x) = \{i : x_i \notin U_i\}$. If
$T \subseteq \iota$ is a finite set with $x_i \in U_i$ for all $i \notin T$, then
$\operatorname{supp}(x) \subseteq T$.

articles.title: Support of an element of a restricted product
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be sets with
subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$. The support of an element $x$ of the restricted product of the $X_i$
with respect to the $U_i$ (a tuple with $x_i \in U_i$ for all but finitely many $i$) is the
finite set of indices $i$ with $x_i \notin U_i$.

articles.title: Chunk map of a piece
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be topological spaces with subsets
$U_i \subseteq X_i$, let $S \subseteq \iota$ be finite, and let $X_S$ be the set of tuples
$x \in \prod_i X_i$ with $x_i \in U_i$ for all $i \notin S$. The chunk map sends each $x \in X_S$
to the same tuple $x$, viewed as an element of the restricted product of the $X_i$ with respect
to the $U_i$ and the principal filter of $\iota \setminus S$; this restricted product consists
of the tuples whose $i$-th entry lies in $U_i$ for every $i \notin S$.

articles.title: The forward map undoes the backward map
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be topological spaces
with subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$, let $P$ be their restricted product (the tuples with
$x_i \in U_i$ for all but finitely many $i$), and let $L$ be the direct limit, over finite sets
$S \subseteq \iota$, of the pieces $X_S$ of tuples with $x_i \in U_i$ for all $i \notin S$. Let
$f : P \to L$ be the forward map, sending $x$ to its class in the piece indexed by its support
$\{i : x_i \notin U_i\}$, and let $g : L \to P$ be the backward map, sending a class to the tuple
carried by any of its representatives. Then $f(g(q)) = q$ for every $q \in L$.

articles.title: Forward map to the direct limit of the pieces
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be topological
spaces with subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$, and let $L$ be the direct limit, over finite sets
$S \subseteq \iota$, of the pieces $X_S$ of tuples with $x_i \in U_i$ for all $i \notin S$. The
forward map sends an element $x$ of the restricted product of the $X_i$ with respect to the
$U_i$ (a tuple with $x_i \in U_i$ for all but finitely many $i$) to the class in $L$ of $x$,
viewed in the piece $X_{\operatorname{supp}(x)}$ indexed by its support
$\operatorname{supp}(x) = \{i : x_i \notin U_i\}$.

articles.title: Transition maps of the pieces
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be topological spaces with
subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$, and for a finite set $S \subseteq \iota$ let $X_S$ be the set of
tuples $x \in \prod_i X_i$ with $x_i \in U_i$ for all $i \notin S$. For finite sets
$S \subseteq T$, the transition map $X_S \to X_T$ of the direct system of pieces sends each tuple
$x$ to itself.

articles.title: Tuples in a piece are eventually in the $U_i$
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a family of
types with subsets $U_i \subseteq X_i$, and let $S$ be a finite set of indices. If a tuple
$x \in \prod_{i \in \iota} X_i$ lies in the piece $X_S$, that is, $x_i \in U_i$ for every
$i \notin S$, then $x_i \in U_i$ for all but finitely many indices $i$.

In other words, $x$ defines an element of the restricted product of the $X_i$ with respect to
the $U_i$.

articles.title: The pieces grow with the finite set
articles.statement:
Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a family of types with
