necessarily smooth, manifold.

articles.title: Integral singular homology as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$ and a
topological space $X$, $H_k(X; \mathbb{Z})$ is the $k$-th singular homology of $X$ with
coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}$, viewed as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module.

articles.title: Aspherical closed 4-manifold
articles.statement:
A closed topological 4-manifold $M$ is aspherical if for
every $k \ge 2$ and every point $x \in M$ the homotopy group $\pi_k(M, x)$ is trivial.

articles.title: Integer homology 4-sphere
articles.statement:
A closed topological 4-manifold $M$ is an integer homology
4-sphere if for every $k \ge 0$ the integral singular homology $H_k(M; \mathbb{Z})$ is isomorphic,
as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module, to $H_k(S^4; \mathbb{Z})$, where $S^4$ is the unit sphere in
$\mathbb{R}^5$.

articles.title: Budney–Gabai knotted three-spheres in $S^1 \times S^3$
articles.statement:
Let $S^1 \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ and
$S^3 \subset \mathbb{R}^4$ be the unit spheres, and fix a point $x_0 \in S^1$. There is a sequence
$e_0, e_1, e_2, \dots$ of smooth embeddings $S^3 \to S^1 \times S^3$ such that the complement of
the image of each $e_n$ is connected, each $e_n$ is homotopic to the standard cross-section
$p \mapsto (x_0, p)$, and for $i \ne j$ the images of $e_i$ and $e_j$ are not smoothly isotopic:
there is no smooth map $H : [0, 1] \times S^3 \to S^1 \times S^3$ such that every slice
$H(t, \cdot)$ is a smooth embedding, $H(0, \cdot)$ has the same image as $e_i$, and $H(1, \cdot)$
has the same image as $e_j$.

## Sources

- R. Budney and D. Gabai, 'Knotted 3-balls in S⁴', Corollary 8.6, arXiv:1912.09029v3 (2021), https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.09029. Problem `budney_gabai_knotted_three_spheres` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Boundary point of the unit disc at a real parameter
articles.statement:
For a real number $r$, this is the
point $e^{2\pi i r}$ of the closed unit disc in $\mathbb{C}$, which lies on its boundary circle.

articles.title: Classification of compact surfaces
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a nonempty, compact, connected Hausdorff
space that is a topological manifold of dimension $2$ with boundary, with charts in the closed
half-plane $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^2 : x_1 \ge 0\}$. Then $S$ is homeomorphic to the unit sphere in
$\mathbb{R}^3$, or there are natural numbers $p$ and $n$ for which one of the following holds:
$p \ge 1$ or $n \ge 1$, and $S$ is homeomorphic to the quotient of the closed unit disc by the
orientable gluing relation with parameters $p$ and $n$; or $p \ge 1$, and $S$ is homeomorphic to
the quotient of the closed unit disc by the non-orientable gluing relation with parameters $p$
and $n$. Each quotient is taken by the equivalence relation that the gluing relation generates,
with the quotient topology.

## Sources

- Jean Gallier & Dianna Xu, *A Guide to the Classification Theorem for Compact Surfaces*, https://www.cis.upenn.edu/~jean/surfclassif-root.pdf. Problem `topological_classification_of_surfaces` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Closed unit disc in the complex plane
articles.statement: The closed unit disc in the complex plane.

articles.title: Gluing relation for the non-orientable normal form
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $p$ and $n$, put
$N = 2p + 3n$ and write $e(t) = e^{2\pi i t}$ for the boundary point of the closed unit disc at
the real parameter $t$. This is the relation on the closed unit disc under which, for every
$x \in [0, 1]$ and every natural number $k < p$, the point $e((2k + x)/N)$ is related to
$e((2k + 1 + x)/N)$, and for every $x \in [0, 1]$ and every natural number $k < n$, the point
$e(-(3k + x)/N)$ is related to $e(-(3k + 3 - x)/N)$; no other pairs are related.

Gluing the disc along it identifies the boundary in the pattern
$a_1 a_1 \cdots a_p a_p c_1 h_1 c_1^{-1} \cdots c_n h_n c_n^{-1}$, where the arcs $h_j$ are left
free.

articles.title: Gluing relation for the orientable normal form
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $p$ and $n$, put
$N = 4p + 3n$ and write $e(t) = e^{2\pi i t}$ for the boundary point of the closed unit disc at
the real parameter $t$. This is the relation on the closed unit disc under which, for every
$x \in [0, 1]$ and every natural number $k < p$, the point $e((4k + x)/N)$ is related to
$e((4k + 3 - x)/N)$ and the point $e((4k + 1 + x)/N)$ is related to $e((4k + 4 - x)/N)$, and
for every $x \in [0, 1]$ and every natural number $k < n$, the point $e(-(3k + x)/N)$ is related
to $e(-(3k + 3 - x)/N)$; no other pairs are related.

Gluing the disc along it identifies the boundary in the pattern $a_1 b_1 a_1^{-1} b_1^{-1}
\cdots a_p b_p a_p^{-1} b_p^{-1} c_1 h_1 c_1^{-1} \cdots c_n h_n c_n^{-1}$, where the arcs $h_j$
are left free.

articles.title: Pardon's theorem: the p-adic integers cannot act faithfully and continuously on a connected 3-manifold
articles.statement:
**Pardon's theorem: the p-adic integers cannot act faithfully and continuously on a
connected 3-manifold.** Let $p$ be a prime and $M$ a connected, Hausdorff, second-countable
topological space with an atlas of charts modelled on $\mathbb{R}^3$, that is, a connected
topological 3-manifold without boundary. Then there is no faithful action of the additive group
$\mathbb{Z}_p$ of $p$-adic integers on $M$ that is jointly continuous as a map
$\mathbb{Z}_p \times M \to M$.

This is the $p$-adic case of the Hilbert–Smith conjecture in dimension three; deducing that every
locally compact group acting faithfully on a connected 3-manifold is a Lie group also needs the
classical reduction to $\mathbb{Z}_p$-actions, which is not part of this statement.

## Sources

- John Pardon, 'The Hilbert-Smith conjecture for three-manifolds', Journal of the American Mathematical Society 26 (2013), no. 3, 879-899, Theorem 1.5. https://doi.org/10.1090/S0894-0347-2013-00766-3. Problem `hilbert_smith_padic_dimension_three` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Cerf's theorem $\Gamma_4 = 0$
articles.statement:
Let $S^3 \subset \mathbb{R}^4$ be the unit sphere. Every
smooth diffeomorphism $f$ of $S^3$ is smoothly isotopic to the restriction of a linear isometry of
$\mathbb{R}^4$: there are an orthogonal matrix $A \in O(4)$ and smooth maps
$F, F' : [0, 1] \times S^3 \to S^3$ such that for every $t \in [0, 1]$ the maps $F(t, \cdot)$ and
$F'(t, \cdot)$ are inverse to each other, and $F(0, p) = f(p)$ and $F(1, p) = Ap$ for all
$p \in S^3$.

## Sources

- J. Cerf, Sur les diffeomorphismes de la sphere de dimension trois, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 53, Springer (1968). Problem `cerf_gamma_four` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Normal subgroups of the identity component of the homeomorphism group of a sphere
articles.statement:
Let
$n \ne 4$ be a natural number and let $S^n$ be the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. Give the
group $\mathrm{Homeo}(S^n)$ of homeomorphisms of $S^n$ the topology induced by the embedding
$h \mapsto (h, h^{-1})$ into pairs of continuous self-maps of $S^n$ with the compact-open
topology, and let $G_0$ be the connected component of the identity in $\mathrm{Homeo}(S^n)$.
If $N$ is a subgroup of $\mathrm{Homeo}(S^n)$ contained in $G_0$ such that $h k h^{-1} \in N$
for all $h \in G_0$ and $k \in N$, then either $N$ is the trivial subgroup or $G_0 \subseteq N$.
In other words, the only normal subgroups of $G_0$ are the trivial one and $G_0$ itself.

This is Ulam's Problem 29 of the Scottish Book, which asked the question for every $n$; the
case $n = 4$ is excluded here. The restriction $n \ne 4$ is the caveat attached to the sphere
case in the Encyclopedia of Mathematics; Epstein's theorem itself is stated for manifolds in
general.

## Sources

- S. Ulam, Problem 29 of the Scottish Book; D. B. A. Epstein, The simplicity of certain groups of homeomorphisms, Compositio Mathematica 22 (1970), 165-173; see the commentary in R. D. Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book, 2nd ed. (Birkhäuser, 2015).

articles.title: Smale conjecture (Hatcher), relative parametrized form
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $X$ be a
compact, Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold with boundary modelled on the
$n$-dimensional half-space, with boundary $\partial X$. Write $S^3$ for the unit sphere of
$\mathbb{R}^4$ and let the orthogonal group $O(4)$ act linearly on it. Let
$F, F' : X \times S^3 \to S^3$ be smooth maps with $F(x, F'(x, p)) = p$ and $F'(x, F(x, p)) = p$
for all $x \in X$ and $p \in S^3$, and let $\psi_\partial : \partial X \to O(4)$ be a continuous
map with $F(b, p) = \psi_\partial(b)\, p$ for all $b \in \partial X$ and $p \in S^3$. Then there
are a continuous map $\psi : X \to O(4)$ that agrees with $\psi_\partial$ on $\partial X$ and
smooth maps $H, H' : X \times [0, 1] \times S^3 \to S^3$ such that for all $x \in X$,
$t \in [0, 1]$ and $p \in S^3$ we have $H(x, t, H'(x, t, p)) = p$, $H'(x, t, H(x, t, p)) = p$,
$H(x, 0, p) = F(x, p)$ and $H(x, 1, p) = \psi(x)\, p$, and $H(b, t, p) = F(b, p)$ whenever
$b \in \partial X$.

Thus each $F(x, \cdot)$ is a diffeomorphism of $S^3$, and $H$ is a smooth isotopy through
diffeomorphisms, relative to $\partial X$, from the family $F$ to the linear family $\psi$.

## Sources

- A. Hatcher, A proof of the Smale conjecture, Diff(S3) = O(4), Ann. of Math. 117 (1983). Problem `smale_conjecture` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: The four-dimensional Smale conjecture is false (Watanabe)
articles.statement:
Write $S^4$ for the unit sphere
of $\mathbb{R}^5$ and let the orthogonal group $O(5)$ act linearly on it. There are an $n \ge 1$,
a compact, Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold $X$ with boundary modelled on the
$n$-dimensional half-space, with boundary $\partial X$, smooth maps
$F, F' : X \times S^4 \to S^4$ with $F(x, F'(x, p)) = p$ and $F'(x, F(x, p)) = p$ for all
$x \in X$ and $p \in S^4$, and a continuous map $\psi_\partial : \partial X \to O(5)$ with
$F(b, p) = \psi_\partial(b)\, p$ for all $b \in \partial X$ and $p \in S^4$, such that the
following fails: there are a continuous map $\psi : X \to O(5)$ that agrees with
$\psi_\partial$ on $\partial X$ and smooth maps $H, H' : X \times [0, 1] \times S^4 \to S^4$
such that for all $x \in X$, $t \in [0, 1]$ and $p \in S^4$ we have
$H(x, t, H'(x, t, p)) = p$, $H'(x, t, H(x, t, p)) = p$, $H(x, 0, p) = F(x, p)$ and
$H(x, 1, p) = \psi(x)\, p$, and $H(b, t, p) = F(b, p)$ whenever $b \in \partial X$.

In other words, the relative parametrized form of the statement that $O(5) \to \mathrm{Diff}(S^4)$
is a homotopy equivalence, the analogue of Hatcher's theorem for $S^3$, does not hold.

## Sources

- T. Watanabe, *Some exotic nontrivial elements of the rational homotopy groups of Diff(S⁴)*, arXiv:1812.02448 (2018). Pairs with the positive S³ statement of Hatcher (Ann. of Math. 117, 1983). Problem `watanabe_four_dim_smale_disproof` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Closed topological 3-manifold
articles.statement:
A closed topological 3-manifold is a nonempty, compact,
connected, Hausdorff, second-countable topological space $M$ together with an atlas of charts,
homeomorphisms from open subsets of $M$ onto open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^3$, whose domains cover
$M$. Since the charts land in $\mathbb{R}^3$ itself rather than in a half-space, $M$ has no
boundary.

articles.title: A closed 3-manifold group with no faithful representation in $GL_4(\mathbb{R})$
articles.statement:
There
is a closed connected topological 3-manifold $M$ with a point $x$ such that no group
homomorphism from the fundamental group $\pi_1(M, x)$ to $GL_4(\mathbb{R})$ is injective.

## Sources

- J. O. Button, *Aspherical 3-manifold groups not in GL(4, k) for any field k*, arXiv:1404.4639 (2014). See the discussion of [Kir97, Problem 3.33] in the K3 problem list. Problem `nonlinear_three_manifold_group` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Bogolyubov's Problem 183 has a negative answer
articles.statement:
Bogolyubov's linearization claim is false:
there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a compact, connected, locally connected topological group $G$
acting continuously on $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that for no homeomorphism $\varphi$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$
is every map $\varphi \circ g \circ \varphi^{-1}$, for $g \in G$, linear.

## Sources

- N. N. Bogolyubov, Problem 183 of the Scottish Book; see the commentary in R. D. Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book, 2nd ed. (Birkhäuser, 2015).

articles.title: Bogolyubov's linearization claim (Scottish Book Problem 183)
articles.statement:
The claim that for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and every compact, connected, locally connected topological group $G$ acting
on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with continuous action map $G \times \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$, there is a
homeomorphism $\varphi$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that for every $g \in G$ there is a linear map
$L_g \colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ with $\varphi(g \cdot x) = L_g(\varphi(x))$ for all
$x \in \mathbb{R}^n$.

This is Bogolyubov's problem in its original form: coordinates can be introduced in which every
transformation of the group is linear.

articles.title: Milnor's exotic 7-sphere
articles.statement:
There is a smooth manifold $M$ modelled on $\mathbb{R}^7$ (a
topological space with a $C^\infty$ atlas of charts into $\mathbb{R}^7$) that is homeomorphic to
the unit sphere $S^7 \subset \mathbb{R}^8$ but is not diffeomorphic to $S^7$ with its standard
smooth structure.

## Sources

- J. Milnor, On manifolds homeomorphic to the 7-sphere, Ann. of Math. 64 (1956), 399-405. Problem `milnor_exotic_sphere_seven` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Smooth Poincaré conjecture in dimension 3
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a nonempty, compact, simply connected
Hausdorff space with a smooth ($C^\infty$) manifold structure modelled on $\mathbb{R}^3$, without
boundary. Then $M$ is $C^\infty$-diffeomorphic to the unit sphere
$S^3 = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^4 : \|x\| = 1\}$ with its standard smooth structure.

## Sources

- G. Perelman, three arXiv preprints 2002-2003 (math/0211159, math/0303109, math/0307245). In dim 3, Smooth ⇔ PL ⇔ Topological via Moise (1952) / Bing (1959). Problem `poincare_3d_smooth` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Topological Poincaré conjecture in dimension 3
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a nonempty, compact, simply
connected Hausdorff space with an atlas of charts to $\mathbb{R}^3$, that is, a topological
3-manifold without boundary. Then $M$ is homeomorphic to the unit sphere
$S^3 = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^4 : \|x\| = 1\}$.

## Sources

- G. Perelman, The entropy formula for the Ricci flow and its geometric applications (arXiv:math/0211159, 2002); Ricci flow with surgery on three-manifolds (arXiv:math/0303109, 2003); Finite extinction time for the solutions to the Ricci flow on certain three-manifolds (arXiv:math/0307245, 2003). Originally conjectured by Henri Poincaré in 1904. Problem `poincare_3d_topological` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Topological Poincaré conjecture in dimension 4
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Hausdorff space with an
atlas of charts to $\mathbb{R}^4$ (a topological 4-manifold without boundary, not assumed
second countable). If $M$ is homotopy equivalent to the unit sphere
$S^4 = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^5 : \|x\| = 1\}$, then $M$ is homeomorphic to $S^4$.

## Sources

- M. H. Freedman, The topology of four-dimensional manifolds, J. Differential Geom. 17 (1982), 357-453. Problem `poincare_4d_topological` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Topological Poincaré conjecture in dimensions at least 5
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 5$ and let $M$ be a
Hausdorff space with an atlas of charts to $\mathbb{R}^n$ (a topological $n$-manifold without
boundary, not assumed second countable). If $M$ is homotopy equivalent to the unit sphere
$S^n = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1} : \|x\| = 1\}$, then $M$ is homeomorphic to $S^n$.

## Sources

- S. Smale, Generalized Poincaré's conjecture in dimensions greater than four, Ann. of Math. 74 (1961), 391-406. Topological case: M. H. A. Newman, The engulfing theorem for topological manifolds, Ann. of Math. 84 (1966) and E. H. Connell, A topological h-cobordism theorem for n ≥ 5, Illinois J. Math. 11 (1967). Problem `poincare_high_dim_topological` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Characterization of topological 3-manifolds
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a topological space equipped
with an atlas of charts modelled on $\mathbb{R}^3$, so that $M$ is locally homeomorphic to
$\mathbb{R}^3$. Then $M$ is a topological 3-manifold if and only if $M$ is Hausdorff and
second-countable.

articles.title: Topological 3-manifold with boundary
articles.statement:
A **topological 3-manifold with boundary**: a Hausdorff, second-countable topological space
locally homeomorphic to the Euclidean half-space `EuclideanHalfSpace 2`.

articles.title: Topological 3-manifold
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a topological space equipped with an atlas of charts,
each a homeomorphism from an open subset of $M$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^3$, whose domains
cover $M$. Then $M$ is a topological 3-manifold if it is Hausdorff and second-countable.

articles.title: Topological 3-manifolds are locally compact
articles.statement:
Every topological 3-manifold $M$ is locally
compact, since $\mathbb{R}^3$ is.

articles.title: Closed topological manifold
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, a closed topological $n$-manifold
is a nonempty, compact, connected, Hausdorff, second-countable topological space $M$ together
with an atlas of charts, homeomorphisms from open subsets of $M$ onto open subsets of
$\mathbb{R}^n$, whose domains cover $M$. Since the charts land in $\mathbb{R}^n$ itself rather
than in a half-space, $M$ has no boundary.

articles.title: Manolescu's disproof of the triangulation conjecture
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 5$
there is a closed connected topological $n$-manifold that is not triangulable.

## Sources

- C. Manolescu, *Pin(2)-equivariant Seiberg–Witten Floer homology and the triangulation conjecture*, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 29 (2016), via the Galewski–Stern and Matumoto reduction. Earlier, the triangulation conjecture was known false in dimension 4 (Casson). Problem `manolescu_triangulation_disproof` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Triangulable closed manifold
articles.statement:
A closed topological $n$-manifold $M$ is triangulable if,
for some natural number $N$, there is a simplicial complex $K$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$ with finitely
many faces such that $M$ is homeomorphic to the geometric realization of $K$, the union of its
faces with the subspace topology from $\mathbb{R}^N$.

For a compact manifold this is the usual notion of triangulability. Requiring finitely many faces
is essential: otherwise any copy of $M$ embedded in $\mathbb{R}^N$ would be the realization of the
complex whose faces are its points.

articles.title: Birkhoff–Kakutani metrization theorem
articles.statement:
Every Hausdorff first-countable topological group is
metrizable.

## Sources

- G. Birkhoff, Compositio Math. 3 (1936), 427-430; S. Kakutani, Proc. Imp. Acad. Tokyo 12 (1936), 4-7, DOI 10.3792/PIA/1195580206.

articles.title: Locally constant compactly supported functions have uniform stabilizers
articles.statement:
A locally constant compactly supported function on a topological group is
invariant under left and right multiplication by elements of some open
neighborhood of `1`.

articles.title: Open profinite completion of a group
articles.statement:
For a group $G$ with a topology, the open profinite
completion of $G$ is the limit, in profinite groups, of the diagram of finite quotients $G/H$,
where $H$ runs over the open finite-index normal subgroups of $G$ and the transition maps are the
projections $G/H \to G/K$ for $H \subseteq K$. Concretely, it is the group of families
$(x_H)_H$ with $x_H \in G/H$ that are compatible under these projections, with the topology of a
subspace of the product of the discrete groups $G/H$.

articles.title: The canonical map has dense image
articles.statement:
For every group $G$ with a topology, the image of the
canonical map from $G$ to its open profinite completion is dense.

No compatibility between the multiplication and the topology of $G$ is assumed.

articles.title: Density of the canonical homomorphism
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group with a topology in which
multiplication is separately continuous. Then the canonical continuous homomorphism from $G$ to
its open profinite completion has dense image.

articles.title: Diagram of finite quotients as profinite groups
articles.statement:
For a group $G$ with a topology, this is
the functor that sends each open finite-index normal subgroup $H$ of $G$ to the finite quotient
group $G/H$ with the discrete topology, regarded as a profinite group, and each inclusion
$H \subseteq K$ to the projection $G/H \to G/K$, $gH \mapsto gK$. It is the diagram of finite
quotients followed by the inclusion of finite groups into profinite groups.

articles.title: Coordinates of the canonical map
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group with a topology. For every $x \in G$
and every open finite-index normal subgroup $H$ of $G$, the $H$-coordinate of the image of $x$
under the canonical map into the open profinite completion of $G$ is the coset $xH \in G/H$.

articles.title: Continuity of the canonical map
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group with a topology in which
multiplication is separately continuous: $x \mapsto ax$ and $x \mapsto xa$ are continuous for
every $a \in G$. Then the canonical map from $G$ to its open profinite completion is continuous.

Joint continuity of multiplication is not needed.

articles.title: Canonical map into the open profinite completion
articles.statement:
For a group $G$ with a topology, this is
the map from $G$ to its open profinite completion that sends $x \in G$ to the family of cosets
$(xH)_H$, where $H$ runs over the open finite-index normal subgroups of $G$.

articles.title: Canonical homomorphism into the open profinite completion
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group with a
topology in which multiplication is separately continuous. This is the canonical map from $G$
to its open profinite completion, $x \mapsto (xH)_H$ with $H$ running over the open
finite-index normal subgroups of $G$, regarded as a continuous group homomorphism.

articles.title: Diagram of finite quotients
articles.statement:
For a group $G$ with a topology, this is the functor from
the category of open finite-index normal subgroups of $G$ to finite groups that sends $H$ to the
quotient group $G/H$ and sends an inclusion $H \subseteq K$ to the projection $G/H \to G/K$,
$gH \mapsto gK$.

articles.title: Open finite-index normal subgroups
articles.statement:
For a group $G$ with a topology, this is the set of
normal subgroups $H$ of $G$ that have finite index and are open in $G$, ordered by inclusion and
viewed as a category: there is a morphism $H \to K$ exactly when $H \subseteq K$.
